overview: Conrad of Montferrat was the defender of Tyre after Hattin and a king-elect of Jerusalem whose assassination shaped Third Crusade politics.
His legacy rests on saving Tyre, without which the Latin East might have collapsed more completely after Hattin.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Conrad of Montferrat was the defender of Tyre after Hattin and a king-elect of Jerusalem whose assassination shaped Third Crusade politics.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: Conrad came from the northern Italian house of Montferrat, a family deeply connected to crusading, Byzantium, and aristocratic marriage networks.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Conrad of Montferrat is remembered as the resourceful and ruthlessly ambitious defender of Tyre, the leader whose energy saved the last major crusader foothold after Hattin and who then maneuvered relentlessly toward the crown of Jerusalem. The sources present a capable and determined commander who arrived at a fortuitous moment, organised the defence of Tyre against Saladin, and made himself indispensable — while pursuing his own claim to the throne with single-minded political guile.

His rivalry with Guy of Lusignan and his maneuvering during the Third Crusade revealed a calculating and self-interested operator, admired for competence but distrusted for ambition. Just as he secured election as king of Jerusalem, he was assassinated in Tyre by the Assassins, in a killing whose sponsorship was much debated and variously blamed on his many enemies.

What the record conveys is a brilliant, energetic, and politically ruthless leader whose ability was matched by his ambition. He is remembered as the savior of Tyre and the king-elect who never reigned — a formidable and divisive figure whose competence kept the crusader cause alive and whose mysterious murder removed one of its most capable, and most grasping, leaders.

contentSections.title: As defender of Tyre and king-elect
paragraphs: Conrad reached Tyre after Hattin and organized the city’s defense against Saladin, preserving a crucial foothold for the crusader states. His rivalry with Guy of Lusignan dominated succession politics during the Third Crusade.

contentSections.title: Death
paragraphs: Conrad was assassinated in Tyre in 1192 shortly after his claim to kingship was recognized.

contentSections.title: Legacy
